why_how.text: Defensive driving means staying prepared for unexpected road users, equipment failures and changing conditions.
Keep a clear view ahead and around the vehicle and remain alert to hazards.
Looking away from the road at an occupant or object inside the vehicle can be dangerous even briefly.
Maintain space around the vehicle for an evasive lane change and know who is beside and behind you.
Use a suitable speed and be ready to slow or stop.
Check mirrors frequently and watch road conditions ahead, to both sides and behind.
Watch for stopping vehicles, people entering or leaving parked cars, pedestrians and bicyclists.
Expect other drivers to make mistakes and watch for reversing lights ahead.
Do not assume a traffic signal will keep a crosswalk safe because other road users may disregard it.
Use particular care near playgrounds, schools and shopping areas where people or bicycles may be hidden.
Other road users may not hear your vehicle, especially in parking lots and crosswalks.
Giving right of way can prevent an unsafe traffic situation.

Do not drive after drinking alcohol, while under a drug’s influence or after taking medicine that can cause drowsiness.

The manual advises sunglasses on bright sunny days.

Driving on badly worn or damaged tires is dangerous and illegal.

Check power-steering fluid regularly and have the system inspected if turning produces a high-pitched sound.
Regularly check headlights, brake lights and turn signals and remove dirt, snow and ice from the lights.
Keep mirrors and windows clean and replace wipers that streak or fail to clear the windshield.
License plates must be clean and unobstructed, with their numbers visible from sixty feet at night.
Registration stickers belong only in the plate’s upper-right corner.

Use a larger following interval for extra safety when traffic allows.
Allow at least four seconds of following space behind a motorcycle.
Allow at least ten seconds of following space behind heavy equipment such as a tractor or dump truck.
Do not cut in front of heavy equipment or tractor-trailers because their greater weight requires more stopping room.
Tailgating is unlawful and can lead to a fine as high as one hundred dollars.
Let a tailgater pass by changing lanes or pulling to the roadside.
Increase space when weather or road conditions are poor.
Allow added space near obstructed driveways, backing vehicles and children playing beside the road.

why_how.text: Reaction time is the interval needed to recognize a situation and move onto the brake pedal.
The manual uses about three-quarters of a second as an educational reaction-time example.
In the manual’s fifty-mile-per-hour example, reaction accounts for about fifty-five feet before braking begins.
The fifty-mile-per-hour example adds about one hundred sixty feet or more after braking begins on dry, clear, level pavement.
The manual’s illustrative total stopping distance at fifty miles per hour on dry, clear, level pavement is about two hundred fifteen feet.
With working brakes and tires on a dry level road, the manual illustrates about two hundred ninety-two feet to react and stop from sixty miles per hour.
The manual illustrates about one hundred four feet of total stopping distance at thirty miles per hour.
The stopping-distance figures are educational examples, and actual distances vary with road, weather and vehicle conditions.
Larger or heavier vehicles, downhill travel and wet, slippery or uneven pavement require additional stopping time.
Large trucks may need twice the stopping distance of passenger vehicles.
When preparing to turn or stop, brake gently and early to warn nearby road users.
Do not keep your foot resting on the brake pedal while driving.
Never pump antilock brakes.
Slow before a curve or any area where the road ahead cannot be seen clearly.

When possible, avoid driving from midnight to six in the morning, and watch for line crossings or rumble-strip contact if you must drive then.
Alcohol can increase drowsiness, and prescription and nonprescription medicine labels should be checked for drowsiness warnings.
Slow when rain first begins because water can mix with road dirt and oil into a slippery film.
Hydroplaning occurs when tires ride on water instead of contacting the road and depends on water, road conditions and speed.
If hydroplaning begins, ease off the accelerator slowly without sudden braking or steering.
In rain or fog, increase spacing and be ready to stop within the visible distance ahead.
Wet leaves can be as slippery as ice.
Use low-beam headlights in fog to reduce glare.
Use turn signals and keep wipers and window defoggers in working condition during wet-weather travel.
If pavement or signposts cannot be seen, slow down and use the road-edge markings for guidance.

why_how.text: Avoid puddles because wet brakes do not work properly; after a large puddle, light braking can dry them until normal operation returns.
On ice or snow, reduce speed, accelerate slowly and leave extra room to stop.
Locking the brakes on ice causes loss of steering control, and a skid calls for steering in the skid’s direction.
Yield to snowplows without crowding them and watch for emergency vehicles.
Bridges and overpasses can freeze before other road surfaces because they lack the ground’s insulation.
When snow is falling, start slowly and gently tap the brakes to check available traction.
Keep the wipers and defroster in good working condition for winter driving.
Remove all snow and ice from the vehicle, including the roof, hood and trunk, so it cannot blow onto vehicles behind.
Failing to remove snow and ice from the vehicle can result in a negligent-operation charge.
Keep the fuel tank at least half full to help prevent the fuel line from freezing.
